newsitem.title: USA: Peru siege sinks when-issued Brady debt prices.
newsitem.headline: Peru siege sinks when-issued Brady debt prices.

text.p: The siege of the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima by a guerilla group late Tuesday sparked a sharp selloff in Peruvian when-issued debt Wednesday, emerging market debt experts said.

"Looking at the Brady market, people have been selling Peru today with some degree of aggressiveness," said Marco Santamaria, vice president of fixed-income research at ING Barings in New York. "Obviously, this is an event of some magnitude and some international import, so people are obviously looking at it very closely."

Late Tuesday, Peruvian rebels stormed the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima and threatened to kill at least 200 hostages, including high-ranking foreign diplomats, unless the government freed jailed comrades of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).
On a when-issued basis, market sources said Peru PDI bonds and the country's FLRBs slid 1-1/2 to 58-1/2 and two points to 54-1/4, respectively.
On a stripped yield spread basis, market sources said Peru (WI) Brady bonds widened to 500 basis points over Treasuries from around 400 to 425 basis points over.

Peru, which is seeking to restructure roughly $4.0 billion in principal and interest with its commercial bank creditors, has analysts divided over whether the hostage situation could delay the Brady closing expected in the first quarter of 1997.

"It might delay the Brady agreement because Peru was going to receive a loan from Japan to make the downpayment on the Bradys," said Carlos Janada, vice president at Morgan Stanley & Co Inc in New York.
However, Santamaria of ING said he does not expect it to impact the timing of the closing of the Brady agreement.
A banking source, who requested anonymity, also added, "We are at the very final stages and I would expect the deal would close in January."
While portfolio managers tend to flee at the first sign of trouble, sources said that long-term direct foreign investors were not likely to pull their money out as quickly, if at all.

"I don't think it will have a serious impact or serious blow to long-term foreign investor sentiment because the groundwork has been laid for a very aggressive foreign investor invitation selling off all the state-owned industries," said Siobhan Manning, Latin American analyst at Santander Investment.
Sources also said they did not expect the hostage situation to hurt the broader Brady market.

"I think people will view this as a localized event. Obviously, the guerillas have been a feature of the Latin American landscape for a long time," said Santamaria, who noted that terrorist groups have been active in Mexico, Colombia and Peru and said investors will have to get used to it.
"I doubt this particular event will change the way that people will look at the region as a whole," he added.
